title: Module Organization
story: Your program has grown to 500 lines across 8 modules. It works, but the organization is messy — logic is in the display module, data types are scattered across three modules, and nobody knows where to find anything. Time to reorganize with clean module boundaries.
why: Well-organized modules follow the Single Responsibility Principle — each module does one thing and does it well, making large codebases navigable, testable, and maintainable by teams.
analogy: Organizing modules is like organizing a kitchen — spices in one cabinet, pots in another, utensils in a drawer. When you need a spatula, you go to the utensil drawer — you don't check every cabinet. A well-organized kitchen (codebase) makes cooking (programming) fast and enjoyable. A messy one makes every task a treasure hunt.
try_it: Take L5-50's Mini Database code and refactor it into clean modules: `database` (Table, Row, CRUD operations), `display` (formatting query results), `query` (find_by, filter logic). Keep main thin — just creating a table, inserting data, and querying. Then add a `reports` module that uses query results to generate summary reports. Notice how easy it is to add features when modules are well-organized.
tips: One module = one folder (conceptually) — if you'd put it in a separate folder on your computer, it deserves its own module
Data modules (models) should have NO behavior — just types. Behavior goes in service modules
If a module name has 'and' or 'or' in it (e.g., `users_and_orders`), split it into two modules
common_mistakes: Putting logic in data modules — `type User` with a `validate()` method in `models` mixes data and validation
Creating upward dependencies — `models` depending on `display` means you can't change display without breaking data
Over-splitting — 20 modules each with one 3-line function is as bad as one module with 20 functions; find the balance
